rules.history_list: a rule of thumb without a trend: watch at 100,000 committed transactions whose undo logs purge has not processed yet, problem at 1,000,000. The size alone says little; a list that keeps growing across refreshes means purge is falling behind, most often because an old read view (a REPEATABLE READ transaction or a long statement) is still open
rules.trx_age: the oldest active transaction is watched at 10 s and a problem at 60 s (as in Sessions)
rules.lock_wait: watch when any transaction is waiting for a lock
rules.purge_state: watch when purge is not running (stopped or disabled)
rules.semaphore: watch when a thread has waited 10 s for an InnoDB latch, problem at 240 s, where InnoDB logs a long semaphore wait (MySQL stops the server once a wait passes 600 s; that limit is fixed in release builds)
rules.pending_io: watch when reads or fsyncs are pending in this snapshot (pending writes are shown but not judged: the page cleaner always has some in flight). One snapshot cannot tell a burst from a backlog: pending reads on every refresh mean queries wait for the storage
rules.redo_mysql: watch when the checkpoint age reaches about 73% of the redo capacity (adaptive flushing at its age limit), problem at about 79% (forced flushing); user writes wait near 84%
rules.redo_mariadb: watch when the checkpoint age reaches 7/8 of Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (InnoDB flushes ahead, about 71% of innodb_log_file_size), problem at Innodb_checkpoint_max_age (writes wait, about 81%)
rules.hit_rate: watch below 99%, problem below 95% with at least 10 pages read from disk per second; judged only with about 10,000 page requests or more in the window
rules.dirty: watch at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct (90 by default); a high share alone is not a stall, waits for a free page and a nearly full redo log are
rules.queue: watch when statements wait in the InnoDB queue, which happens only when innodb_thread_concurrency is above 0 and that many threads are already inside InnoDB

notes: Each read of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS restarts InnoDB's per-second averages for every reader. Statuses are rules of thumb from one snapshot, not verdicts; values that stay high across refreshes matter more than one reading.
